findings.issue: handleListUsers is the only one of AccessHandler's four handlers that does not call h.identity(w, r) before touching the service. handleMe (line 63), handleCreateRequest (line 92) and handleSetAccess (line 130) all guard themselves with `identity, ok := h.identity(w, r); if !ok { return }` as a defense-in-depth check against a misconfigured route (registered without RequireAuth/RequireAdmin in front). handleListUsers skips straight to h.access.ListUsers(r.Context()) and writes the full user list with no such check.
findings.impact: GET /api/v1/admin/users is the handler that returns the most sensitive bulk data in this whole feature — every user's login, display_name, email, role, has_access and request_status in one response. Today it is safe only because BuildRoutes happens to wrap RegisterAdmin's mux with RequireSameOrigin→RequireAuth→RequireAdmin (verified in routes.go and exercised by TestAdminUsers_NoCookies401AndNonAdmin403 / TestAdminUsers_AsAdmin200). But that safety lives entirely in the caller, not in the handler, and it is untested from the handler's own perspective: no test calls handleListUsers (or RegisterAdmin) directly against an unprotected mux. If a future change to BuildRoutes drops the wrap for this one route (a copy/paste edit to the admin block, a refactor that reorders the RegisterAdmin call before the middleware wrap is applied, or a new caller that mounts RegisterAdmin elsewhere) — nothing in access.go itself would stop it from serving the full user directory to an anonymous caller. This directly contradicts the type-level doc comment on AccessHandler (lines 13-16) which explicitly frames "take identity from context" as this handler's own responsibility, something it does for 3 of 4 routes and skips for the 4th without explanation.
findings.recommendation: Add the same `if _, ok := h.identity(w, r); !ok { return }` guard to handleListUsers (the returned identity isn't needed for the call, but the presence check is what matters), so all four routes fail closed the same way if ever mounted without RequireAuth in front. Alternatively, if the team decides handlers should never re-check what middleware already guarantees, remove the identity() calls from the other three handlers instead — but pick one policy and apply it uniformly across the file, and say so in the doc comment.

findings.issue: Task 5's own spec text (tasks/5.md, "What to do" item 1) says route registration should be "методом Register(mux *http.ServeMux) по образцу APIHandler.Register в http.go" — i.e. a single Register method mirroring APIHandler's. The implementation instead exposes two methods, RegisterAccess and RegisterAdmin, split by middleware chain rather than by resource.
findings.impact: Low — the split is well-reasoned and documented in the comment above the two methods (different prefixes need different middleware chains, which a single Register(mux) call can't express without leaking routing decisions into the handler). Functionally correct and matches the Architecture table. But it's an undocumented deviation from the literal task instruction; the task's Post-completion checklist requires recording deviations from spec in decisions.md, and at review time no such entry exists yet.
findings.recommendation: No code change needed — the design is sound. Make sure the decisions.md report for Task 5 explicitly calls out this naming deviation (Register → RegisterAccess/RegisterAdmin) and the reason, per the task's own Post-completion checklist.

findings.issue: AccessHandler.identity() (access.go:167-174) duplicates the same "identity missing → 401 session_identity_missing, fail closed" logic already implemented in middleware.go's resolveAccessState (middleware.go:134-142), just with writeAPIError instead of writeError for the response. Both exist for the same reason (defend against a route mounted without RequireAuth) and both are effectively unreachable in the current wiring.
findings.impact: Minor duplication across two files for the same defensive invariant; a future change to the fail-closed behavior (e.g. the response code or body shape for this case) would need to be made in two places and could easily drift — as it already has: middleware.go uses writeError (auth.go's convention) while access.go correctly uses writeAPIError (http.go's convention) for what is conceptually the identical check.
findings.recommendation: Consider factoring the "identity present and non-blank, else write a fail-closed 401" check into one shared helper in middleware.go that both AccessHandler and RequireAccess/RequireAdmin call, so the convention (and the response format) can't diverge between the two call sites.

findings.issue: writeError (auth.go:708-714) and writeAPIError/writeAPIJSON (http.go:242-250) produce byte-identical output (`{"error": "<code>"}` with the same Content-Type and status handling) — they are not actually incompatible conventions, just two copies of the same function living in different files. This isn't introduced by Task 5, but Task 5's own task file explicitly calls this out as a hard split ("это отдельная, несовместимая конвенция ответа") and routes.go/access.go now sit in the same package as both, wiring together code that follows each one.
findings.impact: Low direct impact — access.go correctly picked writeAPIDomainError/writeAPIError as instructed. But the premise that the two functions are behaviorally different is inaccurate, and having two functions with identical bodies in the same package is a straightforward DRY violation that will only get more confusing as new handler code is added to this package and has to guess which of the two "conventions" to call.
findings.recommendation: Out of this task's stated scope (auth.go is flagged as "existing, don't re-review"), but worth a follow-up ticket: collapse writeError into writeAPIError (or vice versa) now that both live in the same handler package, and update auth.go's callers to use the single function.

clean_check: Verified and found no defects in: (1) middleware chain order in BuildRoutes vs the Architecture table — RequireSameOrigin→RequireAuth→RequireAccess on /api/v1/users/, →RequireAdmin on /api/v1/admin/, RequireAuth-only on /api/v1/access/, all confirmed by reading the actual wrapping order in routes.go and cross-checked against middleware_test.go's TestRequireSameOrigin_Matrix and main_test.go's TestNewMux_AccessChainsAreAttached; (2) CORS→Metrics→mux external wrapper order in main.go — unchanged, diff confirms only newMux's internals changed; (3) normalizePath's new isAdminUserLogin branch — traced index arithmetic by hand against /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access and /api/v1/admin/users (no false-positive collapse of the literal 'users' segment), confirmed no out-of-bounds risk since the i>=2 guard makes parts[i-1]/parts[i-2] always safe, and confirmed it reads from the original `parts` slice rather than the being-mutated `normalized` slice so collapse order doesn't matter; (4) POST /auth/yandex removal — absent from BuildRoutes, no dangling reference; (5) writeAPIDomainError usage in access.go — all four domain-error paths (handleMe, handleCreateRequest, handleListUsers, handleSetAccess) go through it, none use auth.go's writeError; (6) decodeJSON/DisallowUnknownFields wiring for setAccessRequest — single Granted *bool field, matches the edge case in the task; (7) config.go's ContactEmail — follows the exact envOrDefault pattern used by every other field, wired through main.go into NewAccessHandler; (8) cross-file signature check for NewAccessService/NewAccessHandler/BuildRoutes/RouteDeps calls in main.go against their actual declarations — all argument lists and types match; (9) go build ./... and go vet ./... run clean in the project's own Docker image, and go test ./... passes without regressions including internal/service/costing_test.go.
summary: The routing/middleware wiring itself is correct and matches the Architecture table exactly, Decision 18's normalizePath change is correctly implemented and tested, and Decision 17's no-leak contract is preserved end to end. The one substantive finding is that handleListUsers (the single highest-value data-exposure endpoint in this feature) is missing the same identity-presence defense-in-depth check the other three AccessHandler methods have, which is an inconsistency with the file's own stated design and currently relies entirely on routes.go for its safety with no direct test coverage of that fact. The remaining findings are minor: a documented-but-unrecorded naming deviation from the task's literal spec text, and small pre-existing duplication (writeError/writeAPIError, and the identity-guard logic itself) that Task 5's new code touches but doesn't introduce.
